---
title: "What is distillation?"
subtitle: "Teaching a small model with a bigger one"
---

{{< include /_setup.qmd >}}

**Knowledge distillation** trains a small model, the *student*, to imitate a larger one, the
*teacher*. The student is cheaper to run: here the 0.8B answers
`{python} serve["one_at_a_time"]` faster than the 2B, one request at a time. The question is how
much of the teacher's skill survives the trip.

It matters most when there are inputs but no answers. Labelling tens of thousands of function calls
by hand is expensive; here the teacher answers all `{python} n(teacher["rows"])` training queries in
about `{python} f"{teacher['gpu_hours']:.1f}"` GPU-hours. So this project asks what a student can learn **without gold labels**, and compares it
with the same student trained on them.

::: {.column-margin}
The idea goes back to [Hinton, Vinyals and Dean (2015)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.02531). For text,
[Kim and Rush (2016)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.07947) showed that training on the teacher's
generated sequences works on its own.
:::

## How the student is trained

Every method here fine-tunes the same Qwen3.5-0.8B with **LoRA**: the model's weights stay frozen,
and small low-rank matrices are added to every linear layer and trained instead, about 1.4% of the
parameters ([results/sft-cost.md](https://github.com/joaomigueloliveira/qwen-function-calling-distillation/blob/main/results/sft-cost.md)). It fits the 12 GB card with room to spare, and every method shares one setup, so they
differ only in what the student is trained toward.

The loss is computed on the answer tokens only. The prompt (the tools and the query) is context the
student reads, not text it learns to write.

::: {.column-margin}
LoRA: [Hu et al., 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685). The shared setup and why it is untuned:
[ADR 0006](../decisions/0006-shared-training-setup.html).
:::

## Three kinds of distillation

Methods differ along two lines: **who writes the text** the student trains on, and **what the
student is trained toward** at each token of it.

| | Who writes the text | Target at each token | Loss | Extra cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **B**, sequence-level ([page](../experiments/b.qmd)) | the teacher | the token it wrote | cross-entropy | one teacher pass over train |
| **C**, logit ([page](../experiments/c.qmd)) | the teacher | its top 20 probabilities | forward KL | B's pass, plus scoring it |
| **D**, on-policy ([page](../experiments/d.qmd)) | the student | the teacher's probabilities on it | reverse KL | the teacher at every step |

The first column is the line between **off-policy** (B, C: learning from text someone else wrote)
and **on-policy** (D: learning from your own attempts). The second is the line between **hard** and
**soft targets**. Each has its own page:

- [Hard and soft targets](targets.qmd): what the teacher's probabilities add, at one real token.
- [Off-policy and on-policy](on-policy.qmd): why a student that only reads the teacher's text can
  still go wrong on its own, and what grading its own answers costs.

## With labels, for reference

**A** is the same recipe on xLAM's gold answers, the reference for what labels buy. Two more methods
use labels only as a filter on the teacher's answers ([filtered B and C](../experiments/filters.qmd)).
On test-clean, A reaches `{python} story.score("A")` and the label-free B
`{python} story.score("B")`: about `{python} h["share_of_a"]` of A's gain over the untrained
student, without a single label.

::: {.column-margin}
Why label-free is the main question:
[ADR 0007](../decisions/0007-label-free-is-the-main-question.html).
:::
